cues.text: A Roman Deacon of Unusual Learning

Nicholas was born in Rome, the son of a papal official named Theodore, and received an education distinguished enough that contemporaries praised his piety, ability, and eloquence even before he entered formal Church service.
Pope Sergius II made him subdeacon and Pope Leo IV ordained him deacon, and by the pontificate of Benedict III he had become one of the papacy's most trusted advisers.
When Benedict died in April 858, the Emperor Louis II — then near Rome — took a close personal interest in the election.
On April 24 Nicholas was chosen, consecrated, and enthroned the same day in St. Peter's, with the emperor himself in attendance.
A Pope Who Would Not Be Overruled

Nicholas inherited a Christendom he judged dangerously adrift — an empire fractured since Charlemagne's death, bishops he considered worldly and unaccountable, and secular rulers increasingly inclined to treat the Church as an instrument of royal convenience.
He answered with a consistent and forceful assertion of papal authority as a check on exactly that drift.
He restored the deposed Bishop Rothad of Soissons after a French archbishop had removed him without proper cause.
He insisted that bishops retained the right of direct appeal to Rome regardless of local metropolitan objection.
A King's Marriage and an Emperor's Anger

Nicholas's most consequential stand came against King Lothair II of Lorraine, who sought to set aside his wife Theutberga in favor of his mistress and had assembled a compliant synod of local bishops willing to grant the annulment.
Nicholas quashed the ruling outright and deposed the two archbishops who had engineered it.
He held firm when Lothair's brother, Emperor Louis II, marched on Rome and besieged the pope in St. Peter's for two days to force his hand—a confrontation Nicholas survived without capitulating.
It was one of the starkest medieval collisions between spiritual and imperial power.
The Church in the East
Nicholas's reign also coincided with a deepening rift with Constantinople: he supported the deposed Patriarch Ignatius against his replacement, Photius.
Nicholas excommunicated Photius in 863 over what Nicholas regarded as an uncanonical removal—a dispute over authority, procedure, and eventually doctrine.
Historians count it among the opening chapters of the eventual permanent schism between Rome and Constantinople two centuries later.
In the same years, missionaries from Nicholas's Rome and from Constantinople both competed for Eastern Europe's newly converting peoples, including the Bulgarians.
Their ruler Boris sent the pope 106 detailed questions on Christian belief and practice, every one of which Nicholas personally answered.
Legacy
Nicholas died in Rome on November 13, 867, still pope.
He had spent nine years insisting, against kings and emperors alike, that the papacy's authority was not a courtesy extended by secular power.
Instead, it was a trust that secular power was bound to respect.
Historians of the papacy have long ranked him among its most consequential medieval occupants, the pontiff who prepared the theological and institutional ground later reforming popes would build on.

We recognize in Nicholas a shepherd who understood that protecting the vulnerable — a deposed bishop, a discarded wife, a distant king's earnest questions — sometimes requires standing, alone if necessary, against the very powers that expect deference.
